variants.text: <childhood>
<calling>
<turning>

The demon realm does not do childhoods, exactly. {a} was simply *there* one morning in the shadow of the black glass, with a name pinned to their cloak and a job to do: {jobA}. Nobody told them whether it was good or bad. It was, they supposed, just a Tuesday.

{a} remembers the realm's first smell: cinders and hot tea. They remember being handed a bowl of soup and a sheet of rules by a very small, very tired imp, and told, kindly, “Don't worry. Everyone starts here.”

If you ask {a} where they come from, they will tell you a long and vivid story about the Ash Fields, a harsh winter, and a family of seven. None of it is true. They know that. But they tell it so well that nobody has had the heart to mention it.

{a} had never actually hurt anyone, and was, in fact, secretly terrified of the idea. The job, they would say, was mostly standing around looking dreadful, and a great deal of paperwork. “You'd be amazed,” {a} says, “what a good scowl will do.”
Under the horns and the helmet, {a} is soft. The other demons know it. They cover for them, now and then, with a cough or an elbow, whenever the general's attention turns their way.

There is a story in {home} that on the night {a} was born the lamps all burned a little higher. It is probably nonsense. But old women in the market still lower their voices and say: “That one. That's the one the stars looked at.”

From the very first day, people could tell that {a} was *different*. Not better: different. A tilt of the head, a pause before speaking, an odd habit of looking at empty rooms as if somebody had just walked out of them. The old ones said it was fate. The young ones said it was nerves.

{a} was always a little hard to forget. It might have been the eyes. It might have been the way they walked into a room as if to a quiet fanfare. In any case, strangers in {home} tended to remember them for years.

The bone-white face of {a} startled children in {home} for years, until they got to know the Chog behind it, who was, it turned out, the gentlest creature alive, with a very good laugh and a lifelong fondness for puns.
There was always a faint glow about {a}, soft green in the dark. In {home} they used it to find the privy at night. {a} considered it an honour.

The slip said {job}, and {a} stood up a little straighter without meaning to. Somebody at the crossroads was already shouting orders, badly. {a} took a breath, found the nearest line of confused recruits, and said, very quietly, “Right. Let's get you into rows.”

{a} had been a {job} for about a minute when the first recruit asked them what to do. “Stand there,” said {a}, “and look as if you meant to.” It worked. It was the beginning of a very short, very successful career in giving orders to people who wanted them.
“{job},” read {a}, and a dozen small habits slotted into place: the straight back, the quick eye, the careful count of exits. They did not know where they had learned them. They did not need to.

When the summoning came, {a} was in the middle of counting something. Then there was a lantern and a crossroads, and a slip of paper that said {job}. “Well,” said {a}, “at least it's an honest title.” By noon they had found the nearest office, requisitioned a chair and begun, quietly, to be indispensable.

The first thing {a} did in Monadia was look for the ledger. There was always a ledger. They found it in the capital, in a cupboard, under a mop, and by the end of the day it had been balanced for the first time in living memory.
{a} took the slip that said {job} with a nod, as if confirming an order. They were the only Chog at the crossroads who looked relieved to have been given a desk.

{a} woke at the crossroads with the smell of hot metal in their nose and a slip that said {job}. Before they had even found their boots they had picked up a stone and began, absently, to shape it. By the time the sun rose there was a very small, very neat bowl.
“{job},” read {a}, and laughed. It felt right the way a good tool feels right: not exciting, just *correct*. They were at a workbench in {home} by sundown, humming, with sawdust in their whiskers.

The summoning found {a} with a half-finished object in their paws, and carried it through intact. They looked at it, then at the slip that said {job}, and shrugged. “All right,” they said. “From the top.”

{a} was already putting the kettle on when they realised they were in the wrong place. A crossroads. Snow. A slip saying {job}. “Never mind,” said {a}, to a passing stranger. “Sit. Have some tea. We'll sort it out.”

People are always in need of something, thought {a}, reading {job} on the slip. Food. Medicine. Company. It was a pleasant thing to be handed, honestly: a purpose, ready-made, with a counter to stand behind.

The summoning took {a} from a long day behind a counter to a longer one, and gave them a better counter, and a stool, and a lantern. {a} took one look at the queue forming and rolled up their sleeves.

{a} knelt, put a paw to the earth of Monadia and listened. It was cold, a little stony, and promising. “{job},” said the slip, and {a} could not have been happier. By evening they had found a patch, a spade, a spare bucket and a stubborn goat.
Mud suited {a}. When the summoning dropped them in a field at the edge of {home}, in a drizzle, with {job} on a slip, they didn't mind. There's no better place to start than the ground.

They said afterwards that the best part of being summoned was the smell: new-turned soil, wet clover, bread somewhere, wood smoke. {a} the {job} walked into {home} with a spring in their step and a plan for the very first row.

The slip said {job}, and {a} felt something in their chest go *click*, like a key in a lock. This, whatever else it was, was what they had been training for all their life without knowing it. They straightened their coat, tightened their straps, and walked to the guild hall with the quiet, terrified calm of a Chog who has just realised the story is theirs.

“{job},” read {a}. Beside them, someone whooped. Further down the road, a Chog was sitting in the snow with their head in their hands. {a} took a deep breath and said, aloud, to nobody: “Right. I can do that.” It was, on the whole, a very optimistic thing to say.

{a} had always known they would be somebody's hero. They had simply not expected to be summoned to a snowy crossroads for it, in a nightshirt, to learn the news. But {job} was a good word. It had weight. It fit the hand. {a} went off to find a sword.

The demon realm called {a} the way a bell calls a congregation: gently, then insistently. They woke with a title: {job}. They were shown a bed, a bowl, a very short list of rules. “Welcome,” said a small, tired imp. “It's not as bad as it looks.” It was, in fact, worse, but also better.

{a} arrived in the black glass at the start of the season with a slip that said {job}, and for a minute, standing in the great echoing hall, felt very small. Then a dark knight clapped them on the shoulder, and said “First day? Don't worry, nobody ever knows what they're doing,” and handed them a mug.

As yet, {a} has not set out on a single quest. Some say they are waiting for a worthy one. Others say they are simply happier in {home}, with {hobby}, and who could blame them? Quests will find them in time. They always do.
{a} has not yet taken a quest, and says it is on purpose. There is a great deal to be said, {a} says, for doing a small thing well. They are working on a {job}'s lot of small things.

So far {a} has finished {#quests quest/quests} this season, each of them small, each of them done carefully, with a note afterwards in the margin of a pocket-book. “It's not much,” says {a}. “But I like to know what I've done.”
{#quests quest/quests} lie behind {a} now, tidy and stamped. They are not the sort of quests that get songs. They are the sort that get thanked, quietly, by someone with a full pantry.

{a} has completed {quests} quests this season, and the guild clerk has started to recognise their face, which is the highest honour a clerk can pay. They are the sort who turns up early and leaves late, who remembers which notice was whose, and who sometimes, when no one is watching, rewrites the notice-board to be clearer.

{quests} done. The number sat comfortably in {a}'s pocket-book, between a recipe and a drawing of a goose. They had stopped counting at ten, to avoid the pressure, and then had to restart, because, as it turned out, they could not stop.

{quests} quests! The tally on {a}'s wall had reached the ceiling and spilled onto the next one. {a} had walked every road in {home}'s region, slept in four temples, been thanked by two hundred strangers, and still, somehow, had a clean collar. “It's a knack,” they said, modestly.

At this point, {a}'s reputation had grown a bit ahead of them. Children in {home} pointed. Innkeepers kept a table back. The guild clerk had stopped stamping their forms and simply started initialling them. {quests} quests, in all, and counting.

{quests} quests is a number that gets you a statue, or at least a bench. {a} has done more than almost anybody in Monadia this season: more roads, more dungeons, more rescues, more cold soup. They are bone-tired and cheerful and have, quite possibly, never been happier.

Counting stopped being useful around the thirtieth. By {quests}, {a} had become a kind of landmark, someone you gave directions by: “Turn left at the bakery, and if you see {a} going the other way, wave.”
{a} has been carried back to the temple {#fails time/times} this season. It does not bother them as much as it bothers everyone else. “It's a good temple,” says {a}. “The soup's nice.”

The temple healers know {a} by name now. {#fails visit/visits} this season, each one with a different bruise and a better excuse. “Please be more careful,” they say. “I will,” says {a}, and means it, every time.

{fails} trips to the temple this season. {a} has a bed there, effectively, and a mug, and a favourite window. The healers say the secret of {a} is not that they don't fall, but that they always, without fail, get up again, and the other patients take heart from it.
{a} has been knocked flat {fails} times this season, and is still standing. “I'm a slow learner,” {a} says, cheerfully, with a bandage round their head. “But I do learn.”

{a} has not been knocked out once this season, which is either skill, or luck, or an extraordinary talent for being somewhere else when things fall over. The healers are suspicious. The rest are impressed.

When the demons came, {a} was on the wall. {#held time/times} so far, they have held the line with the rest of {home}, with whatever came to hand: a ladle, a ladder, a very large pot. “I wasn't brave,” they say. “I was just there, and they were coming.”
{a} has stood on the walls {#held time/times} this season. Each time the town held, and each time {a} came down afterwards a little taller. It is the kind of thing that changes a person.

{a} was caught in a raid, {#hurt time/times}, and still has the marks: a long scrape on one arm, a notch out of an ear. They are not ashamed of them. “Everyone in {home} has one,” {a} says. “Mine's just bigger.”

{a} has raided the towns of Monadia {#raidsMade time/times}. They are very polite about it. The defenders, who do not know this, are not. {a} has begun to suspect that the whole business is a misunderstanding on both sides.

{a} has set out with a party {#parties time/times}. It suits them. There is a kind of Chog who is only fully themselves in company, and {a} is one: louder, funnier, braver, surer. They are the one who remembers everybody's lunch.

Parties, for {a}, are not a tactic but a temperament. {parties} so far this season. They are good at the bit in the middle of a quest, when the road is long and somebody has to say something to keep spirits up.

[[trains>=1|{a} has sparred {#trains time/times} in the yard at {home}. ]][[trades>=1|They have traded {#trades time/times} in the market, mostly for the pleasure of the haggling. ]][[gossips>=1|And they have exchanged gossip {#gossips time/times}, which is, as {a} is fond of saying, the real business of a town.]]

Between quests, {a} {=likes to wander|drifts about|keeps busy}: {#trains sparring match/sparring matches}, {#trades trade/trades}, {#gossips piece/pieces} of gossip, {#heals patched-up friend/patched-up friends}. {a} says the small things add up to a life.
{a} is only level {level} and in no hurry. “There is plenty of time,” they say. “And somebody has to be the sort who notices the flowers.”
At level {level}, {a} has begun to feel the shape of what they do. The right motion arrives before the thought. It is not mastery. It is the first gentle signal that mastery exists.
Level {level} is a good place to be. You are old enough to know what you are doing, and young enough to be surprised. {a} is enjoying both.
Level {level}. People step aside, now, when {a} walks by, not from fear but from a vague, respectful instinct. {a} has not quite got used to it, and keeps apologising to doorframes.
{a} has reached level {level}, a number that makes veteran soldiers whistle. It has done nothing to their manners. They still wipe their feet.
The guild now calls {a} “{titleName}”, and they pretend to find it embarrassing. They have, in fact, had it written on a small card and pinned inside their coat.
“{titleName},” says the clerk, writing it in the register. {a} blushes. It is a title earned the slow way, one honest day after another, and they are prouder of it than of anything.
{a} has done well for themselves: {gold} rupees tucked away in various pockets, and a sock. They are not sure what to spend it on. “Something sensible,” says {a}, “or a very large cake.”
{a} has very little money. They give most of it away, to strays, to apprentices, to anyone with a sad face and a sound argument. “It'll find its way back,” says {a}, with a shrug. Mostly, it does.
Their Status Window shows {#skillsN skill/skills}: {skillList}. {a} has the measure of {=it|them} the way you know the stairs in your own house, in the dark, by feel.
{skillList}: that is what {a} can do, in the language of the Status Window. It is not everything. It is, they say, enough to be going on with.

Every one of {a}'s six skill slots is filled: {skillList}. It is a rare thing, and the whole of Monadia knows it. When {a} walks into a room, a small hush falls, the hush of professionals recognising one of their own.
The stars have noticed {a}: {#gifts gift/gifts} from the Constellations so far. {a} knows it. They look up sometimes, at dusk, and nod, the way you do to a neighbour across the street.
Somewhere up there, someone is rooting for {a}. {#gifts gift/gifts}, small and exact and perfectly timed. {a} has not been able to say thank you. They are working on it.

And then, of course, there is the thing everyone knows. This season, {a} was the Hero. The one who landed the final blow, who walked into the cracked throne room and came out into a green morning. They don't talk about it much. When asked, they say, “I was just the one at the front.”

{a} broke a seal this season. {slays} of them, in fact. They went into the dark and came out with the dust of a Demon General on their boots, and the country, from the capital to the smallest hamlet, rang with it.

People are saying that {a} might be the one. The bards put their name on lists. The taverns take bets. {a} has taken to wearing a hat, in case anyone recognises them, and the hat has, naturally, made them easier to spot.

{a} fell this season, in the black glass, to one of the Heroes. It was not a dramatic fall. They simply sat down, quietly, and said: “Well. That's that.” Their comrades say it was the bravest thing they ever saw.
